props.title: Cobra Verde
props.initialSlug: Slave trader becomes brutal overseer in West Africa

sections.content: Werner Herzog and Klaus Kinski's final collaboration **Cobra Verde** (1987) stands as a fevered examination of colonialism and madness. Based on Bruce Chatwin's novel "The Viceroy of Ouidah," the film follows a Brazilian bandit who becomes a brutal slave trader in West Africa. Like Herzog's earlier **Aguirre, the Wrath of God** (1972) and **Fitzcarraldo** (1982), it features Kinski as an obsessed outsider whose grandiose ambitions lead to his downfall. The production was notoriously difficult, with Herzog and Kinski's volatile relationship reaching its breaking point amid the harsh filming conditions in Ghana.

sections.content: The film's hallucinatory power comes from Herzog's unflinching portrayal of the West African slave trade and his ability to capture authentic locations and performances from non-professional actors. Like **Apocalypse Now** (1979) and **The Mission** (1986), **Cobra Verde** uses the journey into colonial territories as a metaphor for psychological disintegration. The scenes of Kinski training an army of Amazonian women warriors remain some of the most surreal and striking images in Herzog's filmography.

The film represents the culmination of Herzog and Kinski's five-film partnership that began with **Aguirre** (1972). Their combustible collaboration produced some of the most ambitious and physically demanding productions in cinema history, with both men pushing each other to extremes. In **Cobra Verde**, Kinski's increasingly erratic behavior during filming mirrored his character's descent into megalomania, creating an uncomfortable meta-commentary on power and madness. sections.content: **Cobra Verde** fits into a tradition of films examining colonialism's psychological toll, alongside works like **The Heart of Darkness** (1993) and **Zama** (2017). Herzog's approach differs in its fever-dream intensity and refusal to moralize, instead presenting Francisco Manoel da Silva's story as a descent into primitive chaos. The film's final scene, with Kinski attempting to drag a boat through the surf before collapsing, serves as both a literal and metaphorical end to their legendary partnership.
